# Part II: Data and Learning Systems {.unnumbered}

In conventional machine learning, data is passive. Datasets are gathered, curated, partitioned into training and validation sets, and treated as an exogenous ground truth ($x \sim P_{\text{data}}$). A vision classifier or language model simply inspects this data; its inferences have no causal power to alter the distribution of the images or documents it will encounter tomorrow. If a model misclassifies an image, that error is isolated—it does not change the physical world.

In Physical AI, this assumption collapses entirely. The data distribution of a physical machine is **endogenous**: the machine participates in a closed causal loop where every action changes the state of the physical plant, directly dictating what its sensors will observe next ($s_{t+1} \sim P(s \mid s_t, a_t)$). 

Because the policy creates its own future sensory inputs, errors in physical AI are inherently dynamic and compounding. A minor tracking deviation of two millimeters at step $t$ does not merely produce a single suboptimal step; it shifts the camera's visual perspective, alters the contact mechanics of the gripper, and pushes the machine into unfamiliar physical states. Under standard supervised learning, the policy has never seen demonstrations of how to recover from these perturbed states. As a result, small initial errors compound quadratically over time ($O(T^2 \epsilon)$), rapidly driving the system off its demonstration manifold into catastrophic physical failure.

Part II explores how to engineer data pipelines and training systems that can master this closed causal loop:

* **Data as Physical Experience:** Moving beyond web scrapes to physical demonstration collection. We examine the systems physics of bilateral teleoperation, multi-camera SerDes timestamp synchronization, proprioceptive sensor drift, and why logging human recovery interventions is mandatory to bound compounding covariate shift.
* **Training for Continuous Action:** Formulating policy architectures that can generate high-dimensional continuous trajectories without collapsing into the mean of multi-modal demonstrations. We analyze why Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) and Diffusion Policies succeed where naive step-by-step imitation fails, and decompose the sim-to-real gap into friction hysteresis, compliance, and actuator phase lag.
* **Evaluation as Closed-Loop Reality:** Confronting why offline test-set accuracy is fundamentally decoupled from physical task success. We establish the systems discipline of closed-loop evaluation—measuring real task completion, intervention frequencies, and worst-case execution percentiles under dynamic distribution shift.

Training an embodied policy is not an exercise in abstract curve fitting. It is the systems engineering of teaching an algorithm how to act, recover, and persist in an unforgiving physical world.
